routes.label: Count by the rise of the upper side

question:
The set \(G\) is defined by the points \((x, y)\) with integer coordinates, \(3 \le |x| \le 7,\) and \(3 \le |y| \le 7.\) How many squares of side at least \(6\) have their four vertices in \(G?\)

[Figure 1](figures/2009_AMC_12B_Q25_question_fig1.svg)
solution:
First determine where the four vertices must lie. Within any one block, horizontal and vertical differences are at most \(4\), so the square of the distance between two points is at most
\[
4^2+4^2=32<6^2.
\]
Any two vertices of a square of side at least \(6\) are at least \(6\) apart. Thus at most one vertex can lie in each block, and every eligible square has exactly one vertex in each of the four blocks.

[Figure 1](figures/2009_AMC_12B_Q25_question_fig1.svg)

The two upper vertices must be adjacent. Otherwise their diagonal would lie entirely above the horizontal axis, while the diagonal joining the two lower vertices would lie entirely below it, contradicting the fact that square diagonals intersect. The same argument for the two right-hand vertices shows that the vertices occur around the square in the order upper left, upper right, lower right, lower left. Call them \(A,B,C,D\), respectively.

Let \(k\) be the vertical rise from \(A\) to \(B\). Their heights are integers from \(3\) through \(7\), so \(-4\le k\le4\). Reflection in the vertical axis pairs squares with rise \(k\) with squares with rise \(-k\). We can therefore count \(k=0,1,2,3,4\), then double the counts for positive rises.

Fix such a nonnegative \(k\). If the horizontal change along \(AB\) is \(d\), the clockwise quarter-turn to side \(BC\) gives horizontal change \(k\) and vertical change \(-d\). Accordingly, write the vertices as
\[
\begin{aligned}
A&=(-p-k,q),& B&=(r,q+k),\\
C&=(r+k,-s),& D&=(-p,-s-k).
\end{aligned}
\]
Here the horizontal change along \(AB\) is \(p+r+k\), and the downward change along \(BC\) is \(q+s+k\). These must agree, so
\[
p+r=q+s.
\]
The coordinate restrictions for all four vertices are exactly
\[
p,q,r,s\in\{3,4,\ldots,7-k\}.
\]
For example, both \(p\) and \(p+k\) must be between \(3\) and \(7\), giving \(3\le p\le7-k\); the other three variables have the same restriction.

Conversely, any four integers in this interval satisfying \(p+r=q+s\) produce a square: consecutive side changes are \((d,k)\) and \((k,-d)\), which are quarter-turns of one another, and opposite side changes are their negatives. Its side length is at least \(d=p+r+k\ge6\). Thus these conditions include exactly the eligible squares with rise \(k\). Each square determines its four vertices by their blocks and hence determines all five parameters, so none is counted twice.

Put \(n=5-k\), the number of integers in the interval. As the sum \(p+r\) increases, its numbers of ordered representations are
\[
1,2,\ldots,n-1,n,n-1,\ldots,2,1.
\]
Indeed, each increase in a small sum allows one more choice for the first entry; after the middle sum, the counts reverse. For each sum, \((q,s)\) independently has the same number of choices. We therefore square each representation count and add. The five counts are
\[
\begin{aligned}
N_0&=5^2+2(1^2+2^2+3^2+4^2)=85,\\
N_1&=4^2+2(1^2+2^2+3^2)=44,\\
N_2&=3^2+2(1^2+2^2)=19,\\
N_3&=2^2+2(1^2)=6,\\
N_4&=1^2=1.
\end{aligned}
\]
Rise zero is counted once, and each positive rise has a distinct reflected partner with negative rise. The exhaustive total is
\[
85+2(44+19+6+1)=\boxed{225},
\]
which is choice \(\mathrm{E}\).
